blocks.title: Loops
bullets: Essentially, loops are a way to do something over and over again.

In developing as a programmer, you want to consider how one could improve areas of one's code where one types the same thing over and over again. Imagine where one might want to "meow" 500 times. Would it be logical to type that same expression of `print("meow")` over and over again?
Loops enable you to create a block of code that executes over and over again.

leftPanel.title: A Washing Machine Cycle
leftPanel.description: It repeats the washing, rinsing, and spinning cycles over and over again until the timer hits zero.

blocks.question: What happens if a while loop condition never becomes False?
blocks.answer: The loop will run forever, creating an 'infinite loop'. You can break out of it in the terminal using Ctrl+C.

blocks.title: While Loops
bullets: The `while` loop is nearly universal throughout all coding languages.
In the text editor window, edit your code as follows:

blocks.title: While Loops Example
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: While Loops
blocks.body: Even though this code will execute `print("meow")` multiple times, it will never stop! It will loop forever. When you get stuck in a loop that executes forever, you can press `control-c` on your keyboard to break out of the loop.
bullets: To fix this loop, we can edit our code as follows:

blocks.title: While Loops Example
blocks.code:
i = 3
while i != 0:
    print("meow")
    i = i - 1
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: While Loops
blocks.body: Now our code executes properly, reducing `i` by `1` for each "iteration" through the loop.
bullets: It's best practice in programming to begin counting with zero:

blocks.title: While Loops Example
blocks.code:
i = 0
while i < 3:
    print("meow")
    i += 1
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: While Loops
blocks.body: Notice how `i += 1` is the same as saying `i = i + 1`.

blocks.title: For Loops
bullets: A `for` loop is a different type of loop. To best understand a `for` loop, it's best to begin by talking about a new variable type called a `list` in Python.
A `for` loop iterates through a `list` of items:

blocks.title: For Loops Example
blocks.code:
for i in [0, 1, 2]:
    print("meow")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: For Loops
bullets: What if you wanted to iterate up to a million? It's best to create code that can work with such extreme cases:

blocks.title: For Loops Example
blocks.code:
for i in range(3):
    print("meow")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: For Loops
blocks.body: `range(3)` provides back three values (`0`, `1`, and `2`) automatically.
bullets: Notice how we never use `i` explicitly in our code. In Python, if such a variable does not have any other significance, we can simply represent this variable as a single underscore `_`:

blocks.title: For Loops Example
blocks.code:
for _ in range(3):
    print("meow")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: For Loops
bullets: Consider the following code:

blocks.title: For Loops Example
blocks.code: print("meow\n" * 3, end="")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: For Loops
blocks.body: This code produces three meows, each on a separate line. By adding `end=""` and the `\n` we tell the compiler to add a line break at the end of each meow.

blocks.title: Dictionaries
bullets: `dict`s or dictionaries is a data structure that allows you to associate keys with values.
Where a `list` is a list of multiple values, a `dict` associates a key with a value:

blocks.title: Dictionaries Example
blocks.code:
students = {
    "Hermione": "Gryffindor",
    "Harry": "Gryffindor",
    "Ron": "Gryffindor",
    "Draco": "Slytherin",
}
print(students["Hermione"])
print(students["Harry"])
print(students["Ron"])
print(students["Draco"])
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: Dictionaries
blocks.body: We use `{}` curly braces to create a dictionary. Where `list`s use numbers to iterate, `dict`s allow us to use words.
bullets: How could we print out both values and keys?

blocks.title: Dictionaries Example
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: Dictionaries
bullets: What if we have more information about our students? You can imagine wanting to have lots of data associated with multiple keys:

blocks.title: Dictionaries Example
blocks.code:
students = [
    {"name": "Hermione", "house": "Gryffindor", "patronus": "Otter"},
    {"name": "Harry", "house": "Gryffindor", "patronus": "Stag"},
    {"name": "Ron", "house": "Gryffindor", "patronus": "Jack Russell terrier"},
    {"name": "Draco", "house": "Slytherin", "patronus": None},
]

for student in students:
    print(student["name"], student["house"], student["patronus"], sep=", ")
blocks.expectedOutput: Run this code to see the result.

blocks.title: Dictionaries
blocks.body: This code creates a `list` of `dict`s. Python has a special `None` designation where there is no value associated with a key.
